snip.t: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM): Inappropriate, unexplained myocardial hypertrophy (wall thickness $\ge 15\text{ mm}$ in adults, or $\ge 13\text{ mm}$ with a family history) occurring in the absence of abnormal loading conditions.

Chest pain and exertional syncope: Critical in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) where exertional syncope signifies dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction or ventricular arrhythmias.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a genetic disorder of the heart muscle that causes abnormal thickening, especially of the interventricular septum, leading to impaired filling and dynamic obstruction. It is the leading cause of sudden death in young athletes and presents with exertional symptoms or a harsh systolic murmur.

sections.p: HCM is defined by unexplained left ventricular wall thickness >15 mm (or >13 mm in family members) with a small or normal cavity and no other cause for hypertrophy. Diagnosis relies on echocardiography, cardiac MRI, and genetic testing.

t.b: Shows wall thickness, cavity size, LVOT gradient; confirms obstruction and diastolic dysfunction.
Quantifies hypertrophy, detects fibrosis, and assesses LVOT obstruction when echo is equivocal.
Identifies pathogenic sarcomere mutations; guides family screening.

sections.p: The American Heart Association stages HCM from I (mild hypertrophy) to IV (advanced heart failure). Severity is graded by LVOT gradient, extent of fibrosis, and symptoms.
The primary cause is autosomal dominant mutations in sarcomere proteins. Other contributors include hypertension, aortic stenosis, and metabolic disorders.

t.b: Positive family history raises suspicion and prompts screening.
Shows LV hypertrophy, repolarisation changes, or arrhythmias.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or report exertional dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or sudden death. A harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border that increases with Valsalva is classic.

t.b: Detects harsh systolic murmur, often louder with Valsalva; carotid radiation is uncommon.
Identifies ventricular ectopy or sustained arrhythmias.

sections.p: Key tests assess anatomy, function, and arrhythmia risk. When resources are limited, a focused echo and ECG are essential.

t.b: Measures wall thickness, LVOT gradient, and diastolic function; essential for diagnosis and risk stratification.
Detects LV hypertrophy, repolarisation abnormalities, and arrhythmias; abnormal Q waves may suggest prior infarction.
Assesses arrhythmia burden; a high burden predicts sudden death.
Provides detailed fibrosis assessment; late gadolinium enhancement predicts arrhythmic risk.
Confirms mutation, informs family screening, and may influence therapy decisions.

sections.p: Dynamic LVOT obstruction, arrhythmias, heart failure, and sudden cardiac death are the main threats. Watch for syncope, unexplained chest pain, or new murmurs.

t.b: Suggests significant obstruction or arrhythmia; requires urgent evaluation.
May indicate progression of obstruction or heart failure.
Could signal ventricular arrhythmia; needs ECG and Holter.

sections.p: Treatment targets obstruction, arrhythmia prevention, and symptom relief. Beta‑blockers or non‑dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers reduce heart rate and obstruction. ICDs are indicated for high‑risk patients.

t.b: Reduces heart rate, improves diastolic filling, and lowers LVOT gradient.
Decreases contractility and LVOT gradient; useful when beta‑blocker is contraindicated.
Negative inotrope that reduces obstruction; avoid in severe LVOT obstruction with low EF.
Prevents sudden death in patients with prior arrhythmia, syncope, or high LVOT gradient.

sections.p: Regular clinical review, ECG, and echo every 1–2 years. Family members should be screened. Lifestyle advice includes avoiding extreme exertion and dehydration.

t.b: Avoid competitive sports and dehydration; encourage moderate exercise.
Ensures symptom control and reduces obstruction.

sections.p: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can mimic aortic stenosis, hypertensive heart disease, and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

faq.a: There is no cure, but treatment can control symptoms and prevent sudden death.

faq.q: Is exercise safe for HCM patients?
faq.a: Moderate, non‑competitive exercise is usually safe; high‑intensity or competitive sports are generally discouraged.

faq.q: Do all family members need screening?
faq.a: Yes, first‑degree relatives should be screened because the disease is autosomal dominant.
